slides.title: Make movement part of your sound design
slides.subtitle: SpatialFabric · from cue to space
bullets: 15-minute conversation · 10-minute demonstration · Q&A
One control surface. Two signal paths.
slides.notes: 0:00–0:45. Open with the creative aim: a performer, prop or virtual actor can become a moving source control. This is not a programming talk. We will follow the patch like a sound designer, then operate it live. Say clearly that the demo uses modest listening levels and that there will be time for questions after the ten-minute demo.

slides.title: The problem: two patches to manage
slides.subtitle: Where is the source? Where does its sound go?
bullets: Position patch: which actor controls which renderer object?
Audio patch: which cue reaches which interface output?
Write both down before reaching for Play.
slides.notes: 0:45–1:45. Ask the room to imagine a moving prop with a playback cue. Point out the two questions on the slide. An object number on a spatial processor and an output number on an audio interface can look similar on a screen but mean different things. A good patch sheet connects them deliberately. Avoid suggesting that adding an actor automatically makes a sound spatial.

slides.title: Two lanes, not one
slides.subtitle: Control data and audio travel separately
bullets: Spatial lane: actor → position messages → external renderer
Audio lane: SoundWave → cue player → OS device / channels
The renderer's audio input patch is still your responsibility.
slides.notes: 1:45–3:15. Spend time on this editable diagram. The cyan lane is like automation/control on a console; it carries numbers, not programme audio. The purple lane carries actual samples to an operating-system device. They can work together in a larger system, but SpatialFabric does not guess the connection. If there is no renderer/audio patch at the venue, the demo can prove control packets and local cue routing; it must not pretend to prove spatial rendering.

slides.title: Spatial lane: a moving control surface
slides.subtitle: The patch is actor → binding → object ID
bullets: Actor: the thing you track or animate
Binding: the source label and ID you assign
Adapter: the destination's message language
Output + a real receiver: check what was sent and received
slides.notes: 3:15–4:30. Use console language: an actor is a source fader under automation; a binding is the patch/name/ID; an adapter is the language spoken at the destination. ADM-OSC and Custom are the implemented choices, not a list of separately certified manufacturer integrations. Show that IDs can differ per target: the example uses 1–4 for ADM and 101–104 for Custom. Preview is useful, but UDP receipt is a separate test.

slides.title: A stage is your tape measure
slides.subtitle: Fit the virtual measurement frame to the real room
bullets: Center = zero; each face = one unit in that direction
Size, orientation and axis conventions must agree
Confirm center, front, right and up before a complex move
slides.notes: 4:30–5:45. Point to the box and cardinal positions, not a formula. Its center is not the floor. The default full box is 20 by 15 by 8 metres. Internal forward/right/up coordinates are translated at the protocol boundary. ADM Cartesian and polar share a radius-limited point; a box corner is not an unlimited renderer radius. Ask the audience to make a simple cardinal-point check part of calibration. The decorative floor is not the measurement volume.

slides.title: Listener following changes the viewpoint
slides.subtitle: It does not drag the set around
bullets: Fixed stage: positions are measured from the room
Follow mode: positions are measured from the player/view target
The authored stage stays put; avoid a second transform downstream
slides.notes: 5:45–6:45. Analogy: changing the observer on a plan, not physically moving the venue. The implementation follows the player view-target actor origin/rotation; do not describe this as verified HMD/head tracking or exact camera-eye tracking. Already-relative objects are sent with an identity listener pose, so a downstream system must not apply the same movement twice. In the demo, watch Radar/Output rather than claiming that the separate stereo cue suddenly pans.

slides.title: Audio lane: a separate cue player
slides.subtitle: From imported file to interface output
bullets: Load / prepare: get the samples ready before GO
Playback worker: keep the device's buffer supplied
Windows: WASAPI · macOS backend: Core Audio, not yet certified
This route bypasses Unreal attenuation / submix processing
slides.notes: 6:45–8:15. Explain the backend as a second operator keeping the next tray of audio ready while the editor draws pictures. Preparing media pays the initial decode cost earlier; it does not promise zero onset delay. Samples are paced to the device rate to avoid assuming every interface is 48 kHz. Windows is the validated native platform; Core Audio implementation is not Mac device certification. Designers should not expect Unreal submix/attenuation or ADM metadata to control this separate stream automatically.

slides.title: Channel 0 does not mean everywhere
slides.subtitle: A small patch detail with a large practical consequence
bullets: 0: source 1 → output 1; source 2 → output 2; and so on
1…N: first source channel → only that chosen output
No automatic mono broadcast, stereo downmix or source-channel extraction
slides.notes: 8:15–9:30. Take a stereo cue: corresponding mapping sends left to output 1 and right to output 2. Selecting output 2 alone sends the first/left source channel to output 2, not the right channel. A mono cue in corresponding mode does not appear in every speaker. This is a patching rule, not a loudspeaker renderer. Confirm the interface's real channel ordering at low level before using it in a rig.

slides.title: What happens when you press Play?
slides.subtitle: Request → device start → natural finish or explicit Stop
bullets: A Play request is not yet proof of audible output
Loop repeats; Loop off allows the tail to drain
Auto Replay waits after a natural end; Stop cancels it
Monitoring follows worker events; listen/capture to verify the real patch
slides.notes: 9:30–11:00. Walk the boxes from prepare to request to device start to finish. An invalid selected device should fail rather than quietly choose another. Natural finish drains queued samples; an explicit Stop is a cancellation. Loop and delayed Auto Replay are different behaviors. Monitoring comes from stream lifecycle events, not a fake acknowledgement on every button press, but even a running stream is not proof the physical loudspeaker is connected. OSC reception remains responsive while PIE is paused; replay delay is still not a sample-clock scheduler.

slides.title: Timing: four clocks, not zero latency
slides.subtitle: Measure the complete route you will actually use
bullets: Editor / game frame time
Control-network update and receiver behavior
Cue preparation + device start + output buffer
Driver, converter and downstream audio chain
slides.notes: 11:00–12:15. Frame updates and audio samples are not the same clock. A send-rate setting is a ceiling on update batches, not guaranteed packets per second or synchronized GO across machines. Background editor throttling can make control look slow without changing the audio device's sample rate. The output-latency diagnostic reported zero when unavailable in one run: that is not measured zero delay. Prewarm, choose sensible buffers, and measure end to end with the intended interface/renderer.

slides.title: Build a show-safe patch
slides.subtitle: Be explicit about devices, endpoints and failure
bullets: Choose the intended device; an explicit missing endpoint fails closed
Use loopback first; remote OSC needs a trusted network
Keep a low-level test cue and an independent mute
Save routing, media, engine/plugin revision and a fallback plan
slides.notes: 12:15–13:45. Empty device means the OS default and can change when the computer changes. Explicit selection is preferable when accidental routing would be unsafe. OSC is unauthenticated; the example is local by default and does not enable an editor MCP server. Two applications cannot safely own the same receive endpoint. Cue limits/Force Inline cooking matter for deployment. Keep an independent system mute and rehearsed fallback; this is not a safety-rated show-control transport.

slides.title: What is proven—and what needs a sound check
slides.subtitle: Evidence is a boundary, not a marketing adjective
bullets: UE 5.8 Win64 builds + 26 native regressions
Live OSC/transport checks and independent packet capture
Standalone example: walking pawn, collision, animation and cue decoding
Still verify physical channels, fidelity, latency, exclusive mode and cooked media
slides.notes: 13:45–15:00. Close the talk by separating software evidence from system certification. The published example has a separate silent PIE smoke test, including landing on its outer floor and a capsule blocked by the perimeter. This is useful evidence but not listening/capture verification of the venue. Mac/Linux/other engines and actual packaged codecs still have their own gates. Transition: now we will operate the prepared scene for ten minutes, then discuss how this fits your workflow.

slides.title: 10-minute demonstration
slides.subtitle: One known-good patch, one observation at a time
bullets: 0–2 min: orient the room; Stage / Objects / Radar
2–4 min: read ADM + Custom IDs and a real packet receiver
4–7 min: percussion, stereo groove, loop exit, replay / Stop
7–9 min: follow the player; show the stage stays put
9–10 min: reset safely and recap the two lanes
slides.notes: DEMO 0:00–10:00. Follow DEMO_RUNSHEET.md. Keep all cues manual-start and quiet. If no receiver is available, say that Output is a preview and do not claim a packet-delivery test. If no external spatial renderer/audio patch is present, explicitly explain that moving objects is not panning the separate PCM groove. Avoid the automated live validator on stage: it intentionally tries a missing device and produces an expected error. End by stopping every cue and restoring fixed stage/listener and OSC state. Allow a few seconds to demonstrate the safety floor only if the planned sequence is ahead of time.

slides.title: Questions: where would this sit in your patch?
slides.subtitle: Allow 5–10 minutes if the event schedule permits
bullets: Which sources should follow movement—and which should stay fixed?
Who owns audio routing, timing, mute and recovery?
Which receiver/interface combinations do we need to verify?
slides.notes: Q&A. Invite sound-design and systems questions before implementation details. Useful answers: this is not automatically a binaural renderer; it does not replace a full cue-list/redundancy workflow; a channel ID is not a spatial object ID; physical delay must be measured. Offer to inspect the patch with a sound designer and system engineer rather than promising untested processor or interface support.

slides.subtitle: Appendix · not part of the timed talk
